issue.description:
**Outcome:** Every issue in an approved scope is fireable: template body, graph set, criteria as `criterion` sub-issues ORGANIZE mints, never ticks.

**Measured:** 2026-08-12 — stage-1 admission PASS; criteria CLEAN.

**Fix:**

* Per issue: assess → author → fresh-context verify; all writes via the tracker port (D1, D12).
* One pass, three configured phases off a frozen mandate table, one lookup site, no literals; per-issue markers, `scope:approved` ends it (M2-1, D4, D5, D11).
* Criteria phase mints one `criterion` sub-issue per criterion, create-if-absent on its Check; GROOM's rubric is a sub-issue (M2-3, M2-4).
* Admission then convergence by defect class: three-state verdict, gradability, bounded re-author, dry-round stop, mandate as defect, escalation at raise (D6–D9, M2-6).
* Re-entry = one gap arithmetic, per-surface digests; hygiene applied, forks raised, replays idempotent; test modules, parity, sanitization (D2, D3, D10, M2-2, M2-5, M2-7).

**Rulings:** dated rulings are comments on this issue (2026-08-08…2026-09-05) and on the v0.3 initiative (2026-09-01); 2026-09-07 — tracker is the source of truth, criteria are criterion sub-issues — [ruling](<https://linear.app/duckburg/project/kodezart-v03-scope-orchestration#comment-f7ae1124-1711-480b-a4f0-de7e1d0edaa7>)

**Done when:** every `criterion` sub-issue is Done and the tracker's rollup shows it; the pre-restructure body is the [snapshot](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-74#comment-0e8dd88c-8aa6-44e7-bdaf-dd6ee9069fbe>).

[review finding 2026-09-12 · L2 against Organize contract] **The Organize admission boundary and configured phase vocabulary are present, but the current trunk does not contain/combine them into the lane's required scope Organize node.**

Evidence on `55a87a5`:
- `types/domain/organize.py` has the right strongly typed three-state admission vocabulary (`BUILDABLE | NOT_BUILDABLE | UNVERIFIABLE`), refusal routing, body-revision digest binding, `MandateKind {GROOM,TICKET,CRITERIA}`, and a frozen `MandateSpec` whose label references are qualified/config-resolved rather than literal stage strings.
- KOD-752's settled ruling confirms `queue:approved:ticket` and `queue:approved:criteria` remain the configured machine terminal markers while `scope:approved` is the separate human approval act.
- `chains/organize.py::OrganizeAdmission` correctly gives assess and verify fresh, independent sessions; it rereads issue revision, linked issues, and criterion subissues, uses a selected-base workspace, returns structured output, and binds the result to the exact body digest. It deliberately performs **no tracker writes**.

What is missing is the L2 owner that makes those primitives a graph step. The current chains roster contains `organize.py` only as the admission/judgment boundary—there is no Organize pass/coordinator owning assess→author→fresh-context verify across the three mandates—and the inspected production `composition/passes.py` does not construct an Organize component. Its scheduled prompt passes are legacy/general passes, while dispatch composition constructs FireDispatcher/LifecycleWatcher. Therefore the lane contract “one Organize pass makes every approved scope issue fireable; Organize mints and never ticks” is not reachable through production composition merely because admission types/sessions exist.

**Heal:** create one scope-grain Organize coordinator/node that consumes the already-configured three-row mandate table and the existing `OrganizeAdmission`; do not invent another admission abstraction. For each eligible issue/phase it should: reread the live source revision → assess in a fresh session → route the typed verdict → author only through the canonical tracker writer under the L1 lease → verify in a *new* session against the new revision → apply bounded re-author/stop rules → write the phase's configured terminal marker only after verified convergence. Criteria minting belongs here as criterion subissues, keyed/idempotent, with the already-defined gap/digest arithmetic. Human-decision refusals must leave a legible blocker rather than silently retrying.

**DRY/agent boundary:** keep deterministic work deterministic (mandate lookup, digests, idempotency, gap arithmetic, routing). Keep buildability/spec-quality judgment in the structured agent call. Do not encode semantic defect recognition as substring/path heuristics—the amendment-review finding on PR112/115 is the cautionary example.

**Verification gate:** from the production constructor, run an approved multi-issue scope through GROOM→TICKET→CRITERIA and prove: exactly the configured three mandates; no hard-coded marker strings; assess and verify have no resumed/shared session; body revision drift invalidates admission; a spec-gap takes bounded reauthor; a human-decision refusal stops; criterion subissues mint idempotently; terminal markers land only after verification; and Organize never executes/ticks a fire. L2 remains downstream of L3/L1 authority decisions, so compose it after those contracts are repaired rather than creating temporary bypasses.

Type-safety verdict: the existing domain/admission layer is strong; the missing piece is the **single orchestration owner and production composition**, not more vocabulary.

## Architecture review — type-safety change requested on the organize admission schema

At v0.3 trunk `55a87a5`, the implemented semantic boundary is directionally correct: `chains/organize.py::OrganizeAdmission` runs a fresh structured-output agent session for assess/verify, while `domain/organize.py::admission_route` and `organize_gap` perform only deterministic identity/edge/digest arithmetic afterward. **Keep that split.**

The schema weakens it unnecessarily. `types/domain/organize.py::AdmissionJudgment` exposes one permissive object with `verdict` plus optional `invented_decision`, `missing_artifact`, `pending_blocker_id`, and `refusal_kind`, then `_require_refusal_evidence()` reconstructs the legal state machine after generation. Thus the structured-output schema can ask the model to produce impossible combinations (BUILDABLE with refusal payload, NOT_BUILDABLE without its required decision/kind, UNVERIFIABLE without blocker/evidence) and relies on post-validation to reject them.

**Smallest correction:** make the three verdicts explicit discriminated variants, e.g. `BuildableAdmission`, `RefusedAdmission(invented_decision, refusal_kind, evidence)`, `UnverifiableAdmission(missing_artifact, pending_blocker_id, evidence)`, with common issue identity. Bind `admitted_body_digest` at the caller/result layer as today. `admission_route()` then pattern-matches the variant rather than recovering payload validity from Optionals. Do the same only where a real sum type already exists; this is not a request for class proliferation elsewhere.

This preserves the correct agentic judgment, improves its structured-output schema, and makes invalid states unrepresentable to typed consumers. It mirrors the same correction requested on KOD-79 rather than creating a second style.

**Type-safety verdict:** current model is a regression relative to the guarantees available from Pydantic discriminated structured output. **KISS:** removes cross-field validator branches and downstream `None` recovery. Verification should assert every legal arm round-trips through the agent schema and former illegal combinations fail at the discriminator/schema boundary.

Separate implementation-status note, not a new architecture defect: current trunk contains the admission session and pure gap/routing helpers, but KOD-74 remains Todo and its own audit records that the author/write/phase-marker consumer is still unbuilt. Do not mistake these primitives for a composed ORGANIZE graph step.

[decision 2026-09-07] open forks from the restructure

**Fork — this issue's own labels are the retired stage vocabulary.** KOD-74 carries `queue:approved:ticket` and `queue:approved:criteria`. The 2026-09-01 amendments replace per-stage approval labels with per-issue phase markers ending at `scope:approved`, so these two labels no longer name anything the design has. This pass held labels fixed and did not touch them.

- Option A — leave them: they stand as a record of the v0.2 manual run's approval through those stages, and only new writes use phase markers.
- Option B — remove them: the retired vocabulary leaves the board, and approval state is read from `scope:approved` alone.

Who rules: the ORGANIZE pass once it owns the label vocabulary through the mandate table (KOD-359, KOD-360); the founder may rule sooner.

No other fork arose in this pass: every AC id parsed unambiguously and each criterion already stands as a `criterion` sub-issue with its AC token in the title. The two criteria sitting at Backlog are already ruled — see the [decision] of 2026-09-05 on this issue.
[ruling] → see KOD-752 — option A: the labels stay; they are ORGANIZE's machine phase markers, not retired vocabulary.

Lane fire for the v0.3 scope layer (charter: the v0.3 initiative). Filed 2026-08-07 from the founder charter; consult maturation at the frontier.

**Recorded intent.** Step 1 of a scope run: make every issue in scope **fireable** — stubs and triage items included — before anything executes. Organize = the spec pass as a graph node: per lane, assess → fresh-context adversarial verify → write back to the tracker, gated by the spec rubric (evidence-grounded context, falsifiable deliverables, verification story, self-sufficiency, real dependency edges, provenance footer).

**Behavioral spec (the** <issue id="5eee576d-1af6-48ab-ba1f-47587ca52fc2" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-50/adopt-the-scheduled-routine-prompts-fire-prep-grooming-as-the">KOD-50</issue> **pattern applied):** the manual 2026-08-07 spec sweep of the v0.2 board — its cluster decomposition, its rubric, its assess/verify/write roles, its report-only discipline for structural proposals — is the behavior this node reproduces mechanically. The v0.2 board is the reference scope for the parity demonstration.

**Deliverable sketch (matured at consult):**

 1. The organize node in the L0 graph: judgment surface running agent sessions with explicit grants (v0.2 session-policy discipline), writing specs and dependency edges through the tracker port.
 2. Rubric enforcement: the spec-pass rubric as the node's gate; structural changes beyond spec text (re-parenting, splits, cancellations) are surfaced as proposals for approval, never applied silently — approval stays the human act.
 3. Idempotency: an already-organized scope passes through with no writes. **Corrected 2026-08-08:** the key is [KOD-95](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-95/idempotent-tracker-writes-marker-keyed-comments-assert-then-edit>) D6's — the stage-1 completion label plus assert-then-edit — and not the provenance footer, which is a provenance stamp rather than a coverage guarantee and is absent from bodies judged already sufficient. That issue owns the correction and states why; naming the footer here as the marker was a live instruction to key on the wrong thing.
 4. **Stage-1 semantics (founder, 2026-08-07).** Organize is stage 1 of the staged run: it drives every issue in scope from its pre-state (stub / `queue:triage` / `queue:proposed`) to the **ticket stage label** (name via OperationConfig, e.g. queue:approved:ticket) — a machine-set completion marker, not an approval act (the human approval happened at scope admission via the meta label). The stage barrier is set-level: the run advances to stage 2 (criteria) only when ALL issues under the meta scope carry the ticket stage label — label arithmetic, computed never judged.
 5. **Prep interplay (corrected 2026-08-07).** Organize runs ONLY inside an approved scope run — the scope META label (L1 D5; its own top-layer label, not a queue: member) gates the entire workflow, stage 1 included. Fire prep's independent mandate (grooming/speccing not-yet-approved material) is upstream content preparation, not a stage: it sets no stage labels. When approval lands on well-prepped issues, organize verifies fast and labels; idempotency (item 3) still protects re-entry within and across runs.
 6. **Admission test — the accept condition for setting the ticket stage label on ONE issue (added 2026-08-08 from the reference-scope run).** Item 4 gives stage 1 a barrier but no accept condition: the rubric named in the Recorded intent is a list of qualities, `self-sufficiency` is a heading rather than a predicate, and the fresh-context verify above is specified per LANE. In the run, the question was asked per ISSUE — *could an implementer build this from the issue alone, without inventing a decision?* — and it refused issues that a set-level label check had already passed, producing these refusal classes: a criterion admitting two readings (one of which makes a poll loop non-terminating); a response model the body names nowhere; a probe call site the body names nowhere; a body contradicting its own committed design. Stage 2 already has its accept condition (the <issue id="0f2121ea-dc02-45c6-895a-3f9ed503f1f9" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-66/kodezart-generate-criteria-infeasible-or-mutually-unsatisfiable">KOD-66</issue> gate); stage 1 has none, and a barrier over unverified labels admits a scope that cannot execute — the cost lands in stage 3 as burned iteration budget.
    * **6a. The test, per issue.** Input set: the issue body + the bodies of its linked issues + the repository at the scope base ref. Explicitly NOT the authoring session's output or reasoning — <issue id="0f2121ea-dc02-45c6-895a-3f9ed503f1f9" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-66/kodezart-generate-criteria-infeasible-or-mutually-unsatisfiable">KOD-66</issue>'s information condition ("the generator cannot be its own refuter") applied to specs, where the field that must not cross is the author's own rationale, as `GeneratedCriteriaOutput.reasoning` (`src/kodezart/types/domain/agent.py:295-299`) is for criteria. Mechanism precedent in-repo: `TicketGenerationLoop._review_node` (`src/kodezart/chains/ticket_generation.py:234-293`) builds the reviewer prompt from task + draft only, under its own `reviewer_session_id`. What that precedent does NOT supply and this test requires: there the reviewer session is threaded across rounds (`ticket_generation.py:293`) and accumulates; the admission session is fresh per round (`session_id=None`).
    * **6b. The verdict, three-state.** `AdmissionVerdict(StrEnum)` in a new `src/kodezart/types/domain/organize.py` — `BUILDABLE | NOT_BUILDABLE | UNVERIFIABLE`, never coerced to a boolean. The contrast is live in-repo: the in-fire ticket review's verdict is `TicketReviewOutput.approved: bool` (`src/kodezart/types/domain/agent.py:75-79`), a shape that cannot express "cannot be established either way". One `AdmissionResult` per issue in the same module: `issue_id`, `verdict`, `invented_decision: str | None`, `missing_artifact: str | None`, `pending_blocker_id: str | None`, `evidence: str`. Model validators: `NOT_BUILDABLE` requires a non-empty `invented_decision` — a refusal that cannot name the decision the implementer would have to invent is not a refusal; `UNVERIFIABLE` requires a non-empty `missing_artifact` and `pending_blocker_id`.
    * **6c. Label arithmetic, mirroring the stage-2 precedent.** Only `BUILDABLE` sets the ticket stage label of item 4. `UNVERIFIABLE` routes on an arithmetic clause, the stage-1 analogue of pending-blocker `unverifiable` being a valid stage-2 pass (that ruling is <issue id="1fdb7b23-7dcd-411b-916d-5827bf7fce20" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-75/v03-l3-topology-planner-scope-walker-blockedby-graph-execution">KOD-75</issue>'s consult comment and stays there): the label is set iff the session's `pending_blocker_id` is in fact a `blockedBy` of the issue AND inside the scope — the judgment names the blocker, the arithmetic verifies the edge, and a named blocker that is not a real in-scope edge falls to 6d. `UNVERIFIABLE` is never coerced to `BUILDABLE` and never silently dropped.
    * **6d. Fail route (absent from this lane today).** `NOT_BUILDABLE`, and `UNVERIFIABLE` whose named blocker fails 6c's edge check, route to bounded re-author + re-test rounds with the refusal's `invented_decision` and `evidence` inlined as the re-author's input. Bound: a new `AppConfig` field `organize_max_admission_rounds` (env `KODEZART_ORGANIZE_MAX_ADMISSION_ROUNDS`), shaped like `max_reviews` (`src/kodezart/core/config.py:74`) — `int`, `ge=1`, `le=10` — never a bare literal.
    * **6e. Exhaustion halts; it never passes through.** The shape to avoid is live in-repo: `TicketGenerationLoop._should_continue` (`src/kodezart/chains/ticket_generation.py:320`) routes to `finalize` once the review bound is spent, so an unapproved draft ships anyway. Stage 1 must not reproduce it. Exhausting the bound returns a typed `StageHaltReport` (same new module): `cause: StageHaltCause(StrEnum){ADMISSION_EXHAUSTED, CONVERGENCE_EXHAUSTED}`, `admission_results: list[AdmissionResult]` (the surviving refusals, each already naming its invented decision per 6b) and `surviving_findings: list[SpecFinding]` (7a's shape, empty on this cause); the ticket stage label is not set on those issues, and the barrier of item 4 does not advance — the label is never set anyway, so the barrier can never advance over an unverified label. The scope-level terminal member that names this halt belongs to L6 under <issue id="a4fdc34e-d183-40cf-b77a-16f1459c6c72" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-30/workflow-complete-has-no-outcome-discriminator-review-failure-exit">KOD-30</issue>'s append-only extension convention (<issue id="7db77f39-4c85-48b0-8240-826917474e89" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-78/v03-l6-scope-terminal-per-lane-outcome-vector-initiative-progress">KOD-78</issue> already carries an organize-rejected scope as a terminal class) — consumed here, not defined here.
 7. **Convergence loop — the pass repeats until a verification round comes back dry (added 2026-08-08 from the reference-scope run).** Item 3's "no writes" and the heartbeat's delta pre-query (the initiative's cron section owns both) express a *delivery* fixpoint, priced by a tracker-state read. Neither can see the fixpoint this deliverable needs, because spec quality is not tracker state. In the run, bringing one layer of the board to consistency took repeated passes with diminishing findings, and every pass scoped to an enumerated findings list reproduced its defect class on surfaces the list did not name.
    * **7a. Scope by class, never by list.** A remediation round takes a **defect class** — the rubric items named in the Recorded intent are the class vocabulary — not the findings enumerated by the previous round. A finding is `SpecFinding` in the same new module: `issue_id`, `defect_class` (a member of that vocabulary), `evidence`. A round's input is the set of `defect_class` values seen so far; the enumerated `SpecFinding`s of the previous round are evidence, never the work list.
    * **7b. Stopping condition.** Repeat until a fresh-context verification round over the pass's whole writable surface set returns no finding of any class seen in a previous round — no `INSTANCE` finding **and** no `MANDATE` finding, the distinction deliverable 8 defines and which this condition therefore includes. Explicitly NOT stopping conditions: "the round made no writes" (item 3's idempotency marker) and "the delta pre-query came back empty".
    * **7c. Coverage.** The verification round covers every surface the pass MAY write in this scope run — every issue under the scope — not only the surfaces the round did write. The measured failure mode is a round repairing one surface and falsifying another.
    * **7d. Bound.** `organize_max_convergence_rounds` (env `KODEZART_ORGANIZE_MAX_CONVERGENCE_ROUNDS`), same field shape as 6d. Exhausting it halts the stage with 6e's `StageHaltReport` at `cause = CONVERGENCE_EXHAUSTED`, `surviving_findings` populated and `admission_results` empty — never a silent advance.
    * **7e. Cadence boundary.** This is the in-pass loop that catches write-write skew before the next round consumes bad output. [finding] Stage-1 fireable-ticket pass over M4 (criterion lifecycle & tracker state) — six organizational holes stage 1 could not fill

Filed from the v0.3 battle test's stage 1, which authored/repaired the eight M4 bodies. Each item below is a gap stage 1 either could not close inside its lease or could only close by pinning an interim. Findings only — no labels, no states, no placement changes were made by this pass.

[finding] Stage-1 caught a grooming hole: the scope admits members that can never be fireable, and the stage-1 barrier cannot express that

Filed 2026-08-11 by the v0.3 stage-1 ticket pass working the port-surface milestone. Filed as a CLASS with one specimen, not as a one-issue repair request.

**The hole.** The stage-1 barrier is arithmetic: every issue in the approved scope carries the ticket marker before stage 2 opens. That arithmetic presumes every scoped member is a candidate for an execution-only fire. It is not true of the board as groomed. A scope legitimately contains members that are **records** — a diagnosis, a calibration fixture, a decision of record — whose value is realised by other members being built, never by firing them. The specimen: one of the two members of the port-surface milestone is a founder-authored incident diagnosis whose six remedies are all dispositioned onto other lanes, and whose body is under a pinned no-edit ruling. Stage 1 cannot make it fireable (nothing to author into it), and cannot repair it (the body is principal-authored and refusing to rewrite it is the very rule that member establishes).

**Why it is grooming's and not stage 1's.** The two lawful resolutions are both organizational acts taken before approval: either the member is not a scope member (its content having been absorbed by the lanes that carry it, which here has already happened), or the scope's vocabulary gains a way to say *in scope, not fireable* so the barrier can count it as satisfied without a false stamp. Stage 1 owns neither — it can only author bodies inside a scope handed to it.

**Consequence if left.** Two bad outcomes, no good one: the barrier never closes and stage 2 never opens; or a pass stamps the ticket marker on a member it knows is not a fireable ticket, which is a false completion marker on the exact surface later stages trust. The second is worse than the first, and it is the one a pass under barrier pressure will pick.

**What the rubric member should carry** (owner: the pre-approval mandate rubric under this lane): a disposition for record-shaped members, taken at grooming time and stated as a checklist item — absorbed-and-removed, or admitted with a non-fireable marker the barrier arithmetic counts. Whichever is chosen, the barrier's statement must be written in terms of *members admitted as fireable*, never *all members*.

**Related mechanics gap, same root, worth one line:** the barrier's own marker vocabulary is machine-set completion markers only, so it has no way to express any terminal disposition other than "ticketed". A member that is legitimately done at grooming time has no way to say so to stage 1.

Stage 1 set no label and no state anywhere while recording this.

`[stage-1 ticket pass 2026-08-11 · MACHINE-AUTHORED — a pass's finding, not an approver's act]`

[finding] 2026-08-12, from the stage-1 ticket pass over the run-supervisor lane (KOD-103) — two grooming holes the ticket pass caught and could not fill.

**1 — The stage-barrier owner is unnamed on the board.** The battle-test finding filed on KOD-103 splits into two consequences, and it addresses the first — *a barrier is n-of-m against the ROSTER; every roster member must positively carry the stage marker, and a missing report or an empty verdict is OPEN, never a pass* — to "the stage-barrier owner". No issue on the board declares that it owns barrier arithmetic. The supervisor lane can only observe the resulting shape (it now does: its tally-unmoved signal was widened to a scope arm in the same pass), and observing a wrong barrier is not the same as computing a right one. Placement is this pass's to make: the scope pass owns the stage markers and the barriers over them, so the n-of-m rule belongs on this lane or on its rubric sub-issue, stated once, with the incident as its fixture. Stage 1 will not author it, because inventing an owner is the organizational act grooming holds.

**2 — An exhaustive-disposition claim has no re-trigger.** The supervisor lane's second groomed amendment closes with "the disposition is now exhaustive", true over the findings that existed at that moment. A finding landed on the same issue the next day and sat undispositioned, with nothing on the board able to notice that an exhaustiveness claim had gone stale. The ticket pass dispositioned it by hand — a manual substitution for a step no node owns. The grooming act needs a trigger keyed to *new findings filed against an already-groomed body*, or every exhaustiveness claim it writes decays silently the first time a run files after the pass. Note the shape: the claim's own truth condition is a query over a set that keeps growing, which is why re-derivation and not re-assertion is the only way it stays true.

No labels and no states were set by this pass.

`[finding]` **Stage-2 validator battle test — the criteria-feasibility contract IS drivable standalone over board criteria; the stage-2 node needs exactly five things the composed tree does not ship. Measured 2026-08-11 against the v0.2 union integration branch at `55b5525`.**

**Verdict: DRIVABLE.** One serious attempt, live engine, end to end, exit 0. A scratch clone of the union branch plus a ~200-line harness drove the shipped refuter dispatch and the shipped sweep over one v0.3 board issue's draft criteria (six criteria extracted from that issue's Verification section). No part of the contract was reimplemented.

**What ran, real, unmodified:** the in-repo prompt registry resolving `criteria_validation` against the operation-config bindings (12,589-char refuter prompt rendered); `mint_criteria`; `format_ticket_as_task`; `CRITERIA_VALIDATION_SCHEMA` as the structured-output contract; the agent service over the live client executor at `plan` permission with the eval tool set; `drain`; then `reconcile` → `sweep` → `regeneration_targets` → `demands_regeneration` → `build_artifact`.

**Result:** 6/6 findings returned and reconciled 1:1, 0 contradictions, every stated verdict grounded against its own evidence by `classify_finding` with no `UngroundedVerdictError`, conjunction satisfiable, `regeneration_targets` empty → clean verdict, no regeneration round consumed, artifact built. One criterion came back `feasible` carrying `vacuous_at_base` from a base demonstration the refuter actually ran. **Measured cost of that one issue's validate step: 39 turns, 384 events, ~600 s wall, 2.10 M cache-read + 36.8 k output tokens, 6.64 USD.** That is the per-issue price of stage 2's validate step at real scale, and it is a measured number rather than an argued one.

**So the split is clean: the CONTRACT is drivable, the NODE is not.** `sweep`, `reconcile`, `minimal_conflicting_subsets`, `regeneration_targets`, `demands_regeneration` and `build_artifact` are pure and took zero adaptation. `_validate_criteria_node` could not be called at all — it reads `ExecutionContext.from_configurable`, `current_ticket(state)`, calls `get_stream_writer()` (a LangGraph run context) and returns a `WorkflowState` delta. Driving it required re-assembling render → dispatch → sweep by hand. **X-0 (shape):** extract the render+dispatch+sweep triple behind one callable taking (issue-or-ticket, criteria, base ref) and returning the validation; the graph node becomes a thin wrapper. Everything below is a gap that callable would still have.

**The five things the stage-2 node needs — each one a substitution this harness had to invent:**

**X-1 — criterion identity is not issue-qualified, and the type system refuses to let it be.** `CRITERION_ID_PREFIX = "AC-"` and `CRITERION_ID_PATTERN = ^AC-[1-9][0-9]*$`; `mint_criterion_id(index)` is the single construction site and takes a bare 1-based position. Seven model fields across the lifecycle are `Field(pattern=CRITERION_ID_PATTERN)`, so a `KOD-n-AC-m` id fails at construction on the first model that touches it. The harness therefore minted `AC-1 … AC-6` — run-local ids that collide across every other issue on a shared board. **This is precisely the defect the criterion-lifecycle model records as its motivating observation** (ids minted in an agent's working memory and resolvable by nobody), still live in the type. The prefix, the pattern and the minting site have one owner by design; widening them to carry an issue qualifier is a change at that one site, and stage 2 cannot write a durable checklist without it.

**X-2 — the refuter's input is typed to an in-fire generated ticket, not to a board issue.** The node renders `format_ticket_as_task(current_ticket(state))`, i.e. a `TicketDraftOutput`: title, summary, context, references, `required_changes` (min length 1, `changeType ∈ {create, modify, delete}`), out-of-scope, open questions. A board issue body is markdown prose. The harness hand-mapped one issue into that shape — and **inventing that mapping is exactly what an execution-only stage must not do**: which prose becomes `context` and which becomes a `required_change` is a decision, and I made six of them. Needed: a board-issue → refuter-input adapter, or a second render path that takes the issue body verbatim.

**X-3 — extraction is not machinery; there is no Verification-section reader anywhere.** The brief's "EXTRACT criteria from Verification sections where they exist" has no code behind it. `mint_criteria` consumes `Sequence[DraftedCriterion]`, which only the generation agent produces; nothing in the tree parses an issue body into drafted criteria. The harness hand-extracted six bullets. Note the asymmetry this leaves: `reconcile` enforces a 1:1 correspondence between dispatched ids and returned findings and raises `CriteriaFanInError` on any hole — but **a bullet silently dropped or doubled during extraction is invisible**, because extraction happens before the ids exist. The extractor needs the same correspondence discipline `reconcile` already applies one step later.

**X-4 — `unverifiable`-pending-blocker is admissible by contract and unstampable by type.** The feasibility record carries `missing_resource: str | None` — free prose — and there is **no blocker-identifier field anywhere in the lifecycle** (zero occurrences of a pending-blocker field in `src/`). D6c on this lane rules the stage-1 analogue: the label is set iff the named `pending_blocker_id` is in fact a `blockedBy` edge of the issue AND inside the scope — the judgment names the blocker and the **arithmetic verifies the edge**. At stage 2 that arithmetic is unimplementable today: prose cannot be checked against an edge set. Needed: a typed pending-blocker id on both the finding and the feasibility models, plus the edge check against the scope's `blockedBy` graph — the stage-2 twin of D6c, not a second mechanism.

**X-5 — the write surface does not exist, confirmed by the refuter's own base demonstration.** Zero occurrences of "checklist" in `src/`. `build_artifact` produces the persisted criteria document that goes to a git file on the ralph branch, not to an issue body. Under the ruling that stage 2 writes the checklist INTO the body, the sweep's output currently has nowhere to land. This restates the criterion-lifecycle lane's own deliverable rather than adding to it — recorded here because it was **measured at base by the live refuter** rather than inferred, and because it is the reason a clean sweep still cannot set the criteria marker under the marker's own meaning.

**One behavioural observation for the CRITERIA mandate, from the first real board issue.** The flagged criterion here was flagged because the loop cannot grade a universally-quantified check over an empty set — a "the machine still does X" invariance bullet, which passes at base and therefore discriminates nothing. Board Verification sections are *full* of invariance bullets: 1 of 6 on the very first issue tried. The sweep's consequence for a flag is the forced `soft_signal` downgrade, and the module records the hazard in its own text — `accept_verdict` tests hard-gate membership first, so **a set in which every criterion is flagged can never be rejected**. Over board-extracted criteria that is not a corner case, it is the expected direction of drift, and the CRITERIA mandate's admission test should treat a high flag rate as an authoring-quality signal — the same instrument this lane already applies to the residual rate. (Not demonstrated in this run: the criterion in question was authored `soft_signal` already, so the downgrade changed nothing. The flag was produced live; the downgrade was not exercised.)

**Reproduction:** the harness, the rendered refuter prompt, the raw structured output and the built artifact are retained in the run's job tmp under `bt-validator-harness/`. Base ref `kodezart/integration-v02-full` at `55b5525`. No board state was written by the run beyond this comment; no code was changed.

[fire-ruling] M2-lane-merge — 2026-08-11, v0.3 grooming pass

The ruling of record delegated "one lane or two" to the roadmap. **Ruled: ONE lane, three configured mandates** (GROOM · TICKET · CRITERIA). This is a reviewable design ruling, not an escalation — the call was explicitly delegated.

**The positive ground.** Grooming, stage 1 and stage 2 are one machine: drive every issue in a scope to a labelled condition through an admission test, a set-level barrier, a class-scoped convergence loop, a halt report on exhaustion, and a terminal label. They differ in exactly three configured values — rubric, admission test, terminal marker. Two components whose only differences are configured values is the fork defect one level up, and this board already carries a ruling against forking a system to add a set to it.

**The five grounds for a SPLIT, re-derived rather than averaged, and why each fails or is repaired without one:**

1. *The authorization boundary would become a runtime parameter.* **Refuted.** Which mandate may run is decided OUTSIDE the node, by meta-label arithmetic (the port lane's ancestor walk). That gate is label arithmetic, which is the charter's own meta-label-gating mechanism — not a parameter the node reads about its own authority.
2. *D2's report-only discipline contradicts the grooming mandate's licence to restructure.* **Real** — and repaired by amendment under EITHER design: D2 narrows to "inside an approved scope" (applied to the body this pass). Once narrowed, no live contradiction remains in one lane.
3. *Write-surface sets span containers.* **Handled.** The GROOM mandate declares its own surface set, acquired all-or-nothing and disjoint from any live scope run's — a scope is either being organized or being run. This is the same discipline a split design would have had to give its second lane.
4. *The terminal acts differ in kind.* **True, and it is a row in the mandate table** — `scope:proposed` for GROOM, the two stage markers for the others.
5. *The consumers differ.* **True, and likewise a row.** Three values, one node.

**What IS admitted from the split proposal:** its lane content becomes ONE new sub-issue of this lane — the GROOM mandate's rubric — and its DRY guard holds: `SpecFinding`/`DefectRole`, the convergence loop and its bound, `StageHaltReport`, the three raise sites and their ordering, the admission-verdict types and the gap computation have exactly one definition site, this issue.

**What would flip the ruling:** a measured case where two mandates must hold overlapping write-surface sets simultaneously. Under the all-or-nothing acquisition rule that case is currently unreachable.

[forward-ruling] 2026-08-11, CORRECTED SAME DAY (the earlier revision conflated the grooming pass with the workflow's stage 1) — per the initiative's corrected third [decision] of this date, the organize concept this lane owns SPLITS:

1. **The grooming pass** — pre-approval, triggered by a triaged candidate scope, general and organizational: cross-project/milestone/issue blocker organization, stakeholder consults on open decisions, deadlines, priority and order verification, the measurable-goal check on every issue. **Terminal act: set `scope:proposed`** — the machine's request for authorization. Behavioral spec: the 2026-08-11 grooming run over this very board (parallel deep-readers → competing designs → judged merge under a KISS floor → adversarial verify with fake-edge + dry-implementation tests → one keyed-idempotent board writer → fresh-context board verify).
2. **The in-workflow stage 1** — post-approval, narrow: **fireable ticket bodies per issue and sub-issue, only that**, agent-optimized; admission test stays the dry-implementation test. Stage 2 adds acceptance criteria only, per the feasibility contract.

Whether the two live in one lane or split is the roadmap's call — this comment records the semantics, not the packaging. The general heartbeat's shallow grooming over not-yet-triaged material is unchanged and sets no labels.

`[v02-run-finding]` **"Adopt X as the behavioural spec" produces a paraphrase unless adoption is mechanically checkable. Measured 2026-08-10.**

The organize node's job is to make everything in scope fireable, and a recurring shape of that work is *adopt an existing artifact as the specification*. This board has a live instance, and it did not survive contact.

`KOD-50` was *"adopt the scheduled routine prompts (fire prep + grooming) as the behavioural spec"*, and it is marked Done. The authoritative texts are **42,776** and **29,191** characters. What the repository carries is roughly **6,000** and **4,000** — about a tenth — and they are agent-written condensations, not the adopted text. Nobody noticed for three days, and `KOD-60` then spent its whole life measuring *parity* against the paraphrase, so every parity claim on that lane was measured against the wrong artifact. A later run then rewrote the paraphrase again.

**Why it failed silently.** "Adopt" reads like a copy and grades like a judgment. Every downstream check — the criteria, the parity checklist, the reviewer — asked *does the template cover the behaviours?*, which a competent condensation passes. No check asked *is this the text?* A summarising step is exactly what a language model does well and unprompted, so the failure is the default outcome rather than an unlucky one.

**The rule for this node.** When the organize node specs an issue whose deliverable is *adopt / port / mirror / bring in* an existing artifact, it must emit a **byte-identity criterion**, not a coverage criterion:

> Rendering the shipped artifact against its configuration produces a string byte-identical to the source.

That criterion cannot be satisfied by paraphrase, cannot be satisfied by a well-argued summary, and needs no judgment to grade. Coverage criteria are the wrong instrument for adoption and should be refused by the node rather than authored.

**The one legitimate reason the copy differs, and how it is handled.** These particular texts carry a personal email address and personal handles, and the target repository is public, so a literal copy is not shippable. That is not an argument for paraphrase — it is the reason the identity-as-configuration mechanism exists. The artifact carries the **verbatim prose** with identity tokens replaced by placeholders, and byte-identity is asserted on the **rendered** output, so the private values live in configuration and never in the repository. Where an adoption needs parameterisation, the node specs the substitution surface explicitly and keeps the byte-identity criterion on the rendered form.

**A corollary worth pinning:** an "adopt" issue must record where the source lives and at what version. `KOD-50` did not, and the authoritative text turned out to be a comment on a different issue that supersedes two attached documents on the same issue — discoverable only by reading the whole thread. A source pointer is part of the spec, not context.

## Edge case for the admission test — a criterion can be born undemonstrable, and authoring is where that is caught

**Founder ruling, 2026-08-08.** A criterion requiring an end-to-end run against a real database, in a scope whose grader has neither a database nor a container runtime, **should never have become an acceptance criterion.** The runtime handling for it — flag, record as residual, continue — is specified on KOD-78 and is correct as a safety net. But a safety net catching a routine case means the thing above it is broken. This is that thing.

**It is a distinct defect, and the existing gate cannot see it.** The generation-time sweep catches criteria that are *infeasible* (no implementation satisfies them) and *mutually unsatisfiable* (no implementation satisfies them jointly). This criterion is neither. It is perfectly satisfiable, the code that satisfies it may well be correct, and it is **ungradable by the grader it was written for**. Satisfiability and demonstrability are different properties, and only the first is currently checked.

**The root cause: the environment assumption is invisible.** Every criterion is authored against an assumed environment — one that can run the tests it names, reach the services it exercises, and hold the data it needs. That assumption is almost never written down. It sat in the prose of "run this end-to-end against a real PostgreSQL", where no gate could evaluate it, so it survived authoring, survived the spec pass, survived a fresh-context refutation, and was discovered by an implementer meeting the machine. By then it was too late to re-grain: the criterion was frozen and the only remaining move was to record it as permanently undemonstrable.

**What must exist:**

1. **A criterion carries its environment requirement explicitly** — the class of capability its demonstration needs, in the same vocabulary the runtime probe uses. A criterion that needs nothing beyond the repository and its test suite says so by carrying nothing. This makes an assumption that was previously buried in prose into a value a gate can read.

2. **A scope declares the environments its criteria may be graded in.** Not discovered per-run — declared, so that authoring has something to check against. This is what turns the check mechanical rather than a matter of an author's imagination.

3. **Authoring refuses a criterion whose requirement no declared environment can meet.** Refusal, not a warning: the criterion does not enter the staged set. The author's options are then the right ones rather than the resigned one — re-grain the criterion to something the grader can settle (that the saver is constructed over an async connection and lifespan-managed is inspectable; that the integration test exists and is marked to run where the capability is present is demonstrable anywhere), and bind the live demonstration to the environment that can actually host it, owned by the issue that owns that environment.

**Note what refusal does NOT mean.** The underlying requirement is real — the database path should work, and someone must demonstrate it. Refusing the criterion is not dropping the requirement; it is refusing to write a requirement at a grain nobody in scope can settle. Scope-shrinking would be deleting the demonstration. This is relocating it to where it can happen.

**The health signal this creates, which is the reason to build it.** Residuals remain necessary — environments change, a third-party service dies, a capability that existed at authoring vanishes by execution — so KOD-78's mechanism is not redundant. But a correctly-authored scope should produce them *rarely*. **If residuals are common, this admission test is failing**, and the residual count is therefore a direct measure of authoring quality rather than merely an inconvenience to be tolerated.

**Relation to the admission test already specified here.** Deliverable 6 asks whether an implementer could build the issue from its own text without inventing a decision. This adds the second half of the same question: **could the grader demonstrate it in an environment this scope declares?** Both are properties of the issue rather than of the code, both are checkable at stage 1, and a criterion failing either one must not carry a stage label.

The generation-time half belongs on KOD-66, which owns the satisfiability gate and whose smallest-repair test already distinguishes a fault in the criterion from a fault in the environment — it needs the authoring-time refusal added alongside. A single writer holds that issue as this is written, so it is recorded here for folding in. This also belongs in the per-criterion cross-off edge-case catalogue as a further member; the next writer of that catalogue should assign its number rather than risk a collision.

issue.title: Idempotent tracker writes: marker-keyed comments, assert-then-edit descriptions, check-before-create PRs and issues
issue.description:
**Outcome:** Every tracker write in a scope run is keyed once, at the port, so a re-run edits what exists rather than creating a copy.

**Measured:** 2026-08-07 scope run — a cold re-run of scaffolding would have made a second set of issues, creation being keyed by nothing.

**Fix:**

* Comment upsert keys on a comment's first-line marker: edit the match, create only when none, typed error on two; prefixes from `OperationConfig`, not literals.
* `edit_description` carries the text it replaces — EDITED, UNCHANGED or `StaleWriteError`; with the stage-1 label it is also the organize key, not the provenance footer; a state move is a separate call.
* `upsert_issue` keyed on (`scope_key`, `deliverable_key`) on an adapter-owned carrier; lookup before create.
* `ForgeQuery` on `GitHubAPIClient` beside `PRCreator`/`CIMonitor`: `open_pr_for_head`, `branch_web_url`. Label and state writes read first, skipping a matching value.

Sub-issue of the L4 lane (<issue id="c2ab66ca-a97a-4ba3-9883-d06b76878ab6" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-76/v03-l4-tracker-as-live-run-state-evaluator-write-back-validation-from">KOD-76</issue>). Filed 2026-08-07 from the manual scope run over the reference board.

## Why this exists

The charter rules idempotency for exactly one write — **branch-association lookup precedes branch minting on re-dispatch** (restated as <issue id="1fdb7b23-7dcd-411b-916d-5827bf7fce20" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-75/v03-l3-topology-planner-scope-walker-blockedby-graph-execution">KOD-75</issue> D5) — and one skip: <issue id="3abe7693-0e37-47a2-ab02-026d28f029df" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-74/v03-l2-organize-node-the-spec-pass-as-a-graph-step-make-everything-in">KOD-74</issue> D3's already-organized pass-through. Every other tracker write in a scope run is unkeyed. The consequence observed in the 2026-08-07 run: a cold re-run of that run's scaffolding step would have created a second set of issues for deliverables the first run had already created, because issue creation was keyed by nothing.

Re-entry is only "the same operation as starting" — the charter's resumability ruling — if every write is keyed. This issue makes that true at the port, once, instead of per call site.

## Grounded at `main` @ `92597c0`

* There is no tracker port yet. `src/kodezart/core/protocols.py` declares the forge seam — `PRCreator` (`:282`) and `CIMonitor` (`:305`) — and nothing tracker-shaped. `TrackerPort`, its conformance suite and the in-process fake MCP server double arrive with <issue id="188b3e2c-8b7c-430e-8ec6-27d9a6cf3764" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-57/vendor-neutral-tracker-port-linear-adapter-first-of-n-github-issues">KOD-57</issue>; this issue shapes that port's **write** half and extends that suite.
* Check-before-create is **not expressible** on today's forge seam: `PRCreator` has exactly `create_pr` (`core/protocols.py:285`) and `comment_on_pr` (`:295`). Neither can answer "does an open PR already exist for this head ref?". `GitHubAPIClient` (`src/kodezart/adapters/github_api.py:19`) implements both `PRCreator` and `CIMonitor`, and does its own vendor translation through `extract_owner_repo` (`src/kodezart/domain/git_url.py:38`) — so the missing capability belongs on that adapter, behind a new protocol beside the existing two.

## Deliverables

**D1 — Marker-keyed comment upsert.** `TrackerPort` gains `upsert_comment(*, target, marker, body)`. The marker is the comment body's **first line**, in the convention the manual run used (`[run-state:lane-pr1]` on <issue id="c211686e-0f7c-4bdc-a17d-38080247a104" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-51/pr-1-adapter-reliability-no-ci-classification-transient-404-tolerance">KOD-51</issue>). The port lists the target's comments, finds the one whose first line equals the marker, and **edits** it; it creates only when none exists. A marker is unique on a target: two comments carrying the same marker on one target is a typed error — never a pick-the-newest heuristic. **Composing the marker is the caller's; enforcing its uniqueness is the port's.** A purpose that occurs once per lane composes `(target, purpose, lane)`; a purpose that recurs within a lane composes one further occurrence key, so several live comments of one purpose coexist on one target without ever colliding — the built example is the escalation marker of [KOD-96](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and>) D11d, keyed on its `escalation_key`. Marker prefixes are composed from an `OperationConfig` mapping entry, never string literals in code.

**D2 — Assert-then-edit descriptions.** `TrackerPort.edit_description(*, target, expected, replacement)` carries the exact text it expects to replace. Three outcomes, total:

* `expected` present → replaced, result `EDITED`;
* `expected` absent and `replacement` already present → no write, result `UNCHANGED` (a replay is a no-op, not an error);
* neither present → typed `StaleWriteError` naming the target and the failed anchor, no write.

That single rule delivers both properties this issue needs: replay writes nothing, and a concurrent edit by another writer is **detected** rather than clobbered.

**D3 — Issue creation keyed by deliverable identity.** `TrackerPort.upsert_issue(*, scope_key, deliverable_key, ...)`. `scope_key` is the identity of the run's `ScopeRef` (<issue id="65211d3b-bb35-46f7-9ab4-a86577604bb7" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-73/v03-l1-scope-input-scoperef-tracker-port-container-vocabulary">KOD-73</issue> D1); `deliverable_key` is the stable identity of the thing being delivered. The pair is recorded on the created issue through the port — the carrier is adapter-owned (label, custom field, or a marker line), the port surface stays vendor-neutral. Lookup precedes create; a hit is updated through D2, never duplicated.

**D4 — Check-before-create on the forge.** A new protocol in `core/protocols.py`, beside `PRCreator`/`CIMonitor`, implemented by the same `GitHubAPIClient`:

```python
@runtime_checkable
class ForgeQuery(Protocol):
    """Read-side forge lookups: existing PRs and branch web URLs."""

    async def open_pr_for_head(
        self,
        *,
        repo_url: str,
        head: str,
    ) -> tuple[str, int] | None: ...

    async def branch_web_url(
        self,
        *,
        repo_url: str,
        branch: str,
    ) -> str: ...
```

`open_pr_for_head` returns `(html_url, number)` shaped exactly like `create_pr`'s return (`adapters/github_api.py:172-196`), or `None`. Vendor translation stays in the adapter, per the standing rule that protocols take `repo_url`. This issue delivers the capability and its conformance tests. The landing coordinator (<issue id="fcf71e60-9ca3-4859-a2db-782ae64b5f23" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-77/v03-l5-landing-coordinator-multi-pr-landing-with-ci-folded-in-at-both">KOD-77</issue>) is the caller that must consult `open_pr_for_head` before `create_pr`, and edit the existing PR rather than open a second one. `branch_web_url` is consumed by the lane run-state record (<issue id="fd0a7f05-6186-4668-8898-d10214693efc" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and">KOD-96</issue>).

**D5 — Set-if-different for labels and states.** Label and workflow-state writes read the current value first and issue no write when it already matches. A replay therefore produces no tracker notification and no state-history entry — which is what makes a heartbeat tick over an unchanged scope free rather than noisy.

**D6 — The organize key is the stage label, not the provenance footer.** The v0.2 protocol already rules why the footer cannot carry idempotency: it is a provenance stamp, not a coverage guarantee, and bodies judged already sufficient carry none — so an unstamped-but-sufficient issue would be re-authored on every run. The correct key is the stage-1 completion label plus D2's assert-then-edit on the description. <issue id="3abe7693-0e37-47a2-ab02-026d28f029df" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-74/v03-l2-organize-node-the-spec-pass-as-a-graph-step-make-everything-in">KOD-74</issue> **owns the organize node**; this issue owns only the port-level contract that node must satisfy, and does not edit it.

**D7 — One conformance property, run against every adapter.** <issue id="188b3e2c-8b7c-430e-8ec6-27d9a6cf3764" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-57/vendor-neutral-tracker-port-linear-adapter-first-of-n-github-issues">KOD-57</issue>'s port-level conformance suite gains: *running any writing component twice over the same input leaves the tracker byte-identical to running it once, and creates no second object.* This is the definition of conforming for the write half of the port.

**D8 —** `CriterionAddress`**: the value that resolves a criterion to the place it occupies (the addressing half of E1).** Two lanes write a criterion through an addressing scheme and both name this issue as its owner — the per-criterion tick across every body shape ([KOD-96](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and>) D9) and the untick on amendment ([KOD-97](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-97/criterion-amendment-reconciler-default-upheld-amend-only-on-a-self>) D9). This is that scheme, specified in the board's three layers.

**(i) Domain vocabulary.** A criterion's identity says *which* criterion; it says nothing about *where* it is written. The value that answers the second question is `CriterionAddress`, a frozen `CamelCaseModel` in a new module `src/kodezart/types/domain/criterion_address.py` — one typed partition per module, the `types/domain/consolidation.py` precedent:

* `criterion_id: str` — the `AC-n` identity minted by <issue id="0f2121ea-dc02-45c6-895a-3f9ed503f1f9" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-66/kodezart-generate-criteria-infeasible-or-mutually-unsatisfiable">KOD-66</issue>; referenced, never a copy of the criterion's text.
* `target: str` — the tracker item whose surface carries it.
* `section: str` — the named section it sits under, located by its heading and never by a line offset.
* `shape: CriterionShape` — which of the board's criterion shapes it occupies.
* `anchor: str | None` — the line the criterion occupies, verbatim, for a shape that admits a line-scoped edit; `None` for a shape that does not. Three-state by construction: `None` means *this shape has no writable line*, and never *the line was not found* — that case is the typed resolution error below.

`CriterionShape(StrEnum)` in the same module, total over the shapes this board actually uses: `CHECKBOX`, `DELIVERABLE_CLAUSE`, `VERIFICATION_CHECK`, `LIVE_PROTOCOL`.

**Minted at exactly one site, and recomputed rather than stored.** Exactly one resolver in `src/kodezart/` constructs a `CriterionAddress`, from the target's body read through the port at the moment of the write. A stored address is a second source of truth about a body that changes underneath it. **No writer locates a target by matching criterion text, and no writer scans for checkbox syntax** — those are the two defects this value exists to remove, and both are asserted statically.

Failure is typed and loud: an identity resolving to no line, or to more than one, raises naming the identity and the target, and no write follows. It never degrades into a whole-body rewrite.

**What this deliverable does not decide:** whether a given shape is written in the body at all. Three of the four never are — [KOD-96](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and>) D9b owns that ruling, and this address serves it by making the shape a value a writer can branch on totally rather than a pattern it has to guess.

**(ii) Conformance property**, added to <issue id="188b3e2c-8b7c-430e-8ec6-27d9a6cf3764" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-57/vendor-neutral-tracker-port-linear-adapter-first-of-n-github-issues">KOD-57</issue> D5's suite and run verbatim against every adapter: an address minted from a body read through the port resolves against that same body written back through the port, so an address is valid input to D2's assert-then-edit with `anchor` as `expected`; a body whose surrounding prose is reformatted around an unchanged criterion line resolves that criterion to the same identity and shape; and a body in which the addressed line has moved fails D2's `StaleWriteError` rather than resolving to a neighbouring criterion. Stated at the port, so it binds every future adapter and not only today's.

**(iii) Adapter mapping — Linear, implementation detail of one adapter.** The surface is the issue description read through the port as markdown; `anchor` is that description's line verbatim; `section` is the markdown heading it sits beneath. An adapter whose bodies are not markdown satisfies (ii) by its own means, and nothing in layers (i) or (ii) knows what markdown is.

Done means: a tick, an untick and an amendment on one criterion all resolve their write target through one constructed `CriterionAddress`, and a static check finds no other module locating a write by criterion text or by checkbox syntax.

## Verification

## Groomed amendment — v0.3 roadmap application (2026-08-11)

**M4-95a — a description edit and a terminal state transition must not travel in one call (D2 extension).** New rule, not previously a deliverable anywhere. *Measured:* a single tracker call carrying both a description edit and a workflow-state transition produced a surface whose state and whose text disagreed about what had happened, and the assert-then-edit precondition could not discriminate which half had raced. **Ruled: the two are separate calls, in that order** — the description edit first, under D2's assert-then-edit precondition; the state transition second, applied through the run-event table. A combined call is refused at the port. Ground: assert-then-edit is a precondition on the TEXT; a call that also carries a state has a second effect the precondition does not cover, so the guarantee the mechanism advertises is silently narrower than its callers assume.

**M4-95b — premise flip, corrected rather than anchored.** Any grounding sentence in this body asserting that **no tracker port exists yet** is FALSE at the base: the port, its adapter and its conformance suite are all present, and this issue's deliverables are extensions of a live surface rather than anticipations of one.

**M4-95c — the criteria carriage note on D8 (from the founder's criteria write-back ruling).** D8's addressing resolves a criterion to the surface it occupies. Under that ruling the acceptance-criteria checklist lives **in the issue body itself**, ticked in place at evaluator cadence with the graded sha inline, as a silent edit — so the body checklist IS the Linear adapter's carriage of criterion satisfaction and per-criterion marker-comment streams are retired. Consequences for this issue, and only these: the addressing scheme resolves against the body checklist as a first-class target rather than as a human rendering; D2's assert-then-edit is the mechanism those ticks are written through; and the port vocabulary is unchanged — satisfaction stays identity-addressed and graded-sha-stamped. The single minting site and the whole-set write stay with the criterion-lifecycle model.

**Edge change applied.** The port-lane blocker drops as a redundant order statement: this issue is a member of the criterion-lifecycle model, whose lane fire carries the port edge, and the parent-Done rule covers it. The premise prose stays untouched.

- [ ] `KOD-95-AC-5` (hard, E) · The same scope and deliverable key issued twice yields one issue, the second call returning the existing reference, and the recorded key round-trips through the port.
- [ ] `KOD-95-AC-6` (hard, E) · The forge read side answers the check-before-create question: the open-PR lookup returns the open pull request for a head ref and nothing when there is none, and the branch web URL is composed by the adapter from its own owner and repository extraction; a fake implementing the read side sits beside the existing PR-creator fake.

- [ ] `KOD-95-AC-8` (hard, E) · One fixture body per criterion shape — a checkbox list, deliverables carrying done-means clauses, numbered verification checks, and a live protocol — resolves each criterion by identity to its shape, to its verbatim line where the shape has one, and to no line where it has none, with the no-line reading distinguishable from a failed lookup.
- [ ] `KOD-95-AC-9` (hard, E) · An identity resolving to no line, and one resolving to more than one, each raise a typed error naming the identity and the target and write nothing; neither ever degrades into a whole-body rewrite.

- [ ] `KOD-95-AC-12` (hard, G) · An address is recomputed from the target's body read through the port at the moment of the write and never stored, so no second source of truth about a changing body exists; a fixture supplying a persisted address fails.
- [ ] `KOD-95-AC-13` (hard, E) · The addressing property is stated at the port and run verbatim against every adapter: an address minted from a body read through the port is valid input to the assert-then-edit write with its anchor as the expected text.
- [ ] `KOD-95-AC-14` (hard, G) · The acceptance-criteria checklist in an issue body is a first-class addressing target rather than a human rendering, and criterion ticks are written through the assert-then-edit surface; the port vocabulary stays identity-addressed and graded-sha-stamped (M4-95c).
- [ ] `KOD-95-AC-15` (hard, G) · A single call carrying both a description edit and a workflow-state transition is refused at the port; the two are issued as separate calls in that order, the edit first under its assert-then-edit precondition (M4-95a).

Ticks are the loop's, written in place at evaluator cadence: the box is flipped and a trailing state-and-sha pair appended, and nothing else on the line. A green* `make check` *is this issue's gate, not a criterion.*

[criteria-validation] Stage-2 validation — 2026-08-12 · **PROVISIONAL, pending top-tier re-verification**

*Graded at the writer tier under the recorded tier deviation: independence holds, elevation does not. Claims re-derived, not inherited.*

**Verdicts over 16 criteria: 16 feasible · 0 unverifiable · 0 infeasible.** Conjunction: **satisfiable**; no conflicting subset.

**Forbidden-class screen.** Clean on all six classes.
- AC-6 was checked as the nearest miss and cleared. It reads the forge, but its demonstration is over a fake implementing the read side beside the existing pull-request-creator fake — so it turns on the adapter's own lookup, never on a live pull request's state. Nothing here is graded by a real forge.
- AC-11 recorded as a pinned-literal observation ("exactly one construction site", "no module matching criterion text or checkbox syntax"). Feasible and brittle under the shipped contract; the count can be hit, and it is the single-minting-site invariant this deliverable exists for.

**Identity integrity.** All 16 ids stored verbatim, backtick-protected; no linkification damage in the raw body.

**Writer ruling double-checked, per the tier rule.** S1-95a resolves the premise flip its own groomed amendment left dangling — the amendment asserts the tracker port already exists and names no ref. **CONFIRMED against the code:** the port, its adapter and its consumers are present at the named ref and absent from the default branch. Without that ruling the amendment reads false and every deliverable here reads as an anticipation rather than the extension it is. The ruling sits inside the writer's licence: it names a ref, it invents no deliverable.

**One reading pinned.** AC-12's "never stored" and AC-13's "valid input to the assert-then-edit write" are two halves of one property — the address is recomputed at write time and handed straight to the edit. An implementation that caches an address between read and write satisfies neither; both were graded together for that reason.

`[v02-run-finding]` **Assert-then-edit, measured: 2026-08-10, `KOD-59`.**

A land phase overwrote a human-authored issue description and set the state to Done in the same call. Version history made it recoverable and the founder restored it, so the cost was small — but two things this deliverable owns are worth pinning from it:

1. **Assert-then-edit is the guard.** The write replaced a body it had not read and did not expect; an assertion on the prior content would have refused. Blind description writes are the failure mode, not the loss.
2. **The state change is the part that persisted.** The body was recoverable from version history; **Done on an unreadable spec was not self-correcting** and survived until an adversarial review found it. So a description edit and a terminal state transition must not travel in one call — a failed or unexpected edit must not leave the state moved.

Worth noting the recovery ceiling: the run could not repair its own damage, because version history is not exposed through the write path it used. That makes the assertion the only in-loop protection.

## Cross-model invariants now have an owner — and this issue has one gap to close

[KOD-104](https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-104/criterion-lifecycle-model-cross-member-invariants-as-conformance-tests) owns agreement across the criterion-lifecycle model — how a criterion is addressed, graded, carried, ruled on and counted. It restates no deliverable here; it turns each observed cross-member contradiction into a conformance test, and it moves the write lease from per-document to per-model (its D2, over [KOD-73](https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-73/v03-l1-scope-input-scoperef-tracker-port-container-vocabulary) D6's mechanism). Membership is the `model:criterion-lifecycle` marker, which this issue now carries.

**The gap this issue must close: the criterion addressing scheme.** Two lanes already write a criterion through it — the tick across every body shape, and the untick on amendment — and both name this issue as its owner (the edge-case catalogue's E1 assignment; [KOD-96](https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and)'s own Dependencies section says so outright). D1–D7 here carry no such deliverable, so those pointers dangle and D9's tick has no write target.

What it has to be, stated as the property [KOD-104](https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-104/criterion-lifecycle-model-cross-member-invariants-as-conformance-tests) D7 will test rather than as a design: a value that resolves a criterion id to the surface, line and shape it occupies — across checkboxes, Deliverables with "done means" clauses, numbered Verification checks and live protocols — minted at exactly one site, with no writer ever locating a target by matching criterion text or by scanning for checkbox syntax.

Not an edit to this body; the deliverable belongs to whoever next holds the model lease.

issue.description:
**Outcome:** the ruling is a dated comment on this issue and the affected criterion is unblocked.
**Fork:** <issue id="45ffebde-e6c3-43cc-9ab5-e78fc0be641b" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-451/kod-75-ac-16-the-dispatch-target-is-the-issue-itself-no-marker-is">KOD-451</issue> requires an issue outside the approved scope to be "refused at plan time rather than reaching the walk". <issue id="d2b3ac56-8fc2-42c7-b5b4-95f6077d1d6e" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-425/kod-75-ac-3-a-lane-is-ready-iff-it-is-approved-and-every-in-scope">KOD-425</issue>'s Do puts the `scope:approved` self-or-ancestor cascade inside the READY predicate in chains/scope_walker.py, and services/scope_planning.py states as its contract that it establishes no approval and leaves it to the walker. Measured at 8257113: `execution_approved` is read in chains/scope_walker.py and nowhere else in src; the two-root container with only the first root approved dispatches the approved one and drops the other with `exclusions == []`, no clause and no log; and a wholly unapproved scope returns outcome empty_eligible_set with empty eligible, exclusions and snapshot — a report that compares EQUAL to the same scope with every criterion met. "Not approved" is today indistinguishable from "nothing to do".
**Options:** 1. Approval stays walker-owned as <issue id="d2b3ac56-8fc2-42c7-b5b4-95f6077d1d6e" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-425/kod-75-ac-3-a-lane-is-ready-iff-it-is-approved-and-every-in-scope">KOD-425</issue> pins it; <issue id="45ffebde-e6c3-43cc-9ab5-e78fc0be641b" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-451/kod-75-ac-16-the-dispatch-target-is-the-issue-itself-no-marker-is">KOD-451</issue>'s clause is read as "never reaches dispatch", and the walker records each unapproved member as an exclusion under the existing ExclusionClause.NOT_APPROVED and logs it, so an unapproved scope is legible as such. 2. Approval moves to plan time: read_scope_plan establishes the cascade and refuses, typed, naming the unapproved keys, so an unapproved member never reaches the walk — <issue id="d2b3ac56-8fc2-42c7-b5b4-95f6077d1d6e" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-425/kod-75-ac-3-a-lane-is-ready-iff-it-is-approved-and-every-in-scope">KOD-425</issue>'s Do is amended, and the partially-approved container is ruled with it (refuse the whole plan, or plan over the approved members only). 3. Split: the plan reader establishes the cascade as a fact on the snapshot without refusing, the walker excludes under NOT_APPROVED, and a refusal is raised only when no member of the scope is approved.
**Pinned interim:** the shipped behaviour — approval read in the walk, unapproved members silently absent. No code moves on <issue id="45ffebde-e6c3-43cc-9ab5-e78fc0be641b" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-451/kod-75-ac-16-the-dispatch-target-is-the-issue-itself-no-marker-is">KOD-451</issue> until this is ruled.
**Rules:** founder
**Source:** the 2026-09-08 refutation on <issue id="45ffebde-e6c3-43cc-9ab5-e78fc0be641b" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-451/kod-75-ac-16-the-dispatch-target-is-the-issue-itself-no-marker-is">KOD-451</issue>, reproduced in the integration worktree. Distinct from <issue id="49dff0c9-44ec-4399-b1fc-3af0d70752f7" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-751/ruling-who-owns-the-approval-barrier-that-refuses-a-scope-holding-an">KOD-751</issue>, which asks who owns the barrier refusing a scope that holds an open decision or a Backlog criterion.
**Done when:** the ruling is a dated comment here, <issue id="45ffebde-e6c3-43cc-9ab5-e78fc0be641b" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-451/kod-75-ac-16-the-dispatch-target-is-the-issue-itself-no-marker-is">KOD-451</issue> is unblocked and rerun against it, and <issue id="d2b3ac56-8fc2-42c7-b5b4-95f6077d1d6e" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-425/kod-75-ac-3-a-lane-is-ready-iff-it-is-approved-and-every-in-scope">KOD-425</issue>'s Do is amended if approval moves.
